title: First words
goal: Greet people, ask how they are, say yes and no, thank someone and apologise politely in Sindhi.
intro:
Sindhi conversations open warmly and at length: a greeting, then several polite questions about health and family. In Sindh the everyday greeting is **السلام عليڪم** (assalāmu ʿalaikum), and almost every sentence to someone you respect is softened with **سائين** (sāīṃ, 'sir') or **ادا** (adā, 'brother').

In this unit you'll learn greetings, yes and no, please and thank you, sorry, and the difference between polite **توهان** (tavhāṃ) and intimate **تون** (tūṃ). Learn the phrases as whole chunks and say them aloud — and start practising the implosive sounds ɗ and ɠ from the very first day.

vocab.note: The standard greeting in Sindh at any time of day. Note Sindhi spelling with ڪ.
m. منهنجي طرفان سلام = give (them) my regards.
جي ها = yes (polite); جي سائين = yes sir. Said alone with rising tone: 'pardon?'
Also a tag 'right?' at the end of a sentence.
f. The most common Sindhi 'thank you'.
m. Sindhi form of Urdu shukriya.
معاف is usually pronounced 'māf'. To a friend: معاف ڪر māf kar.
ٺيڪ آهي = OK, fine.
Said alone, 'chaṅgo!' = OK then! Also used when taking leave.
ڀلي! = sure, go ahead. ڀلي ڪري آيا = welcome.
Said to guests arriving; very warm and very Sindhi.
Same meaning as خدا حافظ; both common.
m. The great Sindhi honorific, for men of any status; added after names (علي سائين) or at the end of a sentence. Feminine: سائڻ sāiṇi (less common).
m. Used for any man your age or older, even strangers: ادا، ٻڌو! 'Brother, listen!'
f. The polite way to address a woman.
Default with anyone you don't know well and with elders. Takes plural verbs.
Friends, children, family of your age or younger. Rude with strangers.
Also heard as 'kīaṃ'.
m. ڇا حال آهي؟ = How are things?
خوش آهيو؟ 'Are you well?' is a standard greeting question. Often said 'khush'.
m. خير سان = (I'm) fine, all is well; خير آهي = it's nothing / all good.
m. شڪر آهي = thank God (I'm well).

grammar.title: Word order: subject – object – verb, with آهي 'is' at the end
grammar.body:
Sindhi puts the **verb at the end** of the sentence: 'I tea drink', 'this my house is'. The most common verb of all is **آهي** (āhe) 'is', which changes its ending to match the subject:

مان … آهيان (āhiyāṃ) — I am
تون … آهين (āhīṃ) — you (intimate) are
هو / هوءَ … آهي (āhe) — he / she is
اسين … آهيون (āhyūṃ) — we are
توهان … آهيو (āhyo) — you (polite) are
هو … آهن (āhin) — they are

The negative 'is not' is usually **ناهي** (nāhe), with the same endings: ناهيان nāhiyāṃ 'I am not'. Questions keep the same order; just raise your voice at the end.

examples.en: Ali drinks tea. (tea comes before the verb)

grammar.title: Polite and intimate 'you': توهان / تون (and اوهان)
grammar.body:
Sindhi has two main words for 'you'. **توهان** (tavhāṃ) is polite: use it with strangers, elders, teachers, shopkeepers, in-laws — and with anyone when in doubt. It always takes **plural** verb forms (آهيو āhyo), even for one person. **تون** (tūṃ) is intimate: for close friends, younger siblings and children. Using تون with a stranger sounds rude.

You will also see and hear **اوهان** (avhāṃ) — a variant of توهان, common in writing and in some regions; it means exactly the same. Strictly speaking the direct (subject) forms are **توهين / اوهين** (tavhīṃ / avhīṃ) and توهان/اوهان are the oblique forms used before postpositions, but in everyday speech **توهان** is used for both, and that is what this course does.

Respect is also shown with words of address: **سائين** (sāīṃ) for men, **ادا** (adā) 'brother', **ادي** (adī) 'sister'. Adding them costs nothing and makes you sound warm and well-mannered.

examples.en: Are you well? (polite, more formal/written style)

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Ayaz, a young man, meets his older neighbour Ghulam Hussain outside their building in Hyderabad.

lines.speaker: Ayaz
lines.native: شڪر آهي، سائين. توهان ڪيئن آهيو؟
lines.roman: shukur āhe, sāīṃ. tavhāṃ kīeṃ āhyo?
lines.en: Thank God, sir. How are you?

lines.speaker: John
lines.native: مهرباني، سائين. توهان سان ملي ڏاڍي خوشي ٿي.
lines.roman: meharbānī, sāīṃ. tavhāṃ sāṃ mile ɗāḍhī xushī thī.
lines.en: Thank you, sir. Very nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: John
lines.native: ٿوري ٿوري. معاف ڪجو، آهستي ڳالهايو.
lines.roman: thorī thorī. māf kajo, āhistī ɠālhāyo.
lines.en: A little. Sorry — please speak slowly.

lines.speaker: Ghulam Hussain

lines.roman: kā ɠālhi nāhe. chaṅgo, xudā hāfiz!

culture: Greetings in Sindh are unhurried. After السلام عليڪم people ask about your health, your family and your work, often several times over — answering each with شڪر آهي or مهرباني. Men usually shake hands (often with both hands, or placing the right hand on the heart); between men and women a nod with the hand on the heart is the safe choice. Sindhi Hindus, in Sindh and in India, often greet with رام رام (rām rām) or جهوليلال (jhūlelāl), after the river-saint revered on Cheti Chand. Calling older people سائين, ادا or ادي, or a relative's title (چاچا, ماسي) even if they are not related, is normal and kind.

tip.title: The verb goes last
tip.body:
- Sindhi puts the verb at the **end**: مان ٺيڪ آهيان is literally 'I fine am'.
- **آهيان** = am (with مان), **آهيو** = are (with توهان), **آهي** = is.
- The question word **ڪيئن** 'how' sits just before the verb: توهان ڪيئن آهيو؟
- 'Not' joins the verb: **ناهيان** 'am not', **ناهي** 'is not'.
tip.pattern: مان + ٺيڪ + آهيان  ·  توهان + ڪيئن + آهيو؟

sentences.native: مان ٺيڪ آهيان، توهان ڪيئن آهيو؟
sentences.roman: māṃ ṭhīku āhiyāṃ, tavhāṃ kīeṃ āhyo?

lessons.title: Yes, no, please and thank you

tip.title: Yes, no and please
tip.body:
- **ها** = yes; **جي ها** is the polite yes, **جي نه** the polite no.
- **نه** = no / not. At the end of a sentence it also means 'right?': ٺيڪ آهي نه؟
- **مهرباني** is the everyday 'thank you'; **شڪريو** is a little more formal.
- **مهرباني ڪري** 'please' goes at the start of a request.

lessons.title: Talking to a friend, a sir, a sister

tip.title: Polite توهان, friendly تون
tip.body:
- **توهان** (polite) → verb **آهيو**: strangers, elders, shopkeepers — and anyone when in doubt.
- **تون** (intimate) → verb **آهين**: close friends, children, younger siblings. With a stranger it sounds rude.
- Add warmth with **سائين** 'sir', **ادا** 'brother', **ادي** 'sister' — even to strangers.

sentences.en: Are you well? (to a close friend)
You're OK, right? (to a close friend)
How are you, brother? (to a close friend)

tip.title: Answering "how are you?"
tip.body:
- Sindhis rarely answer with just 'fine'. Say **الحمدلله** or **شڪر آهي** 'thank God', or **خير سان** 'all well'.
- Then turn the question back: **توهان ٻڌايو؟** 'and you?' (lit. you tell).
- **سلام** on its own is a quick, friendly 'hi'.

sentences.en: Thank God (I am well). How are you?

sentences.native: ادي، شڪر آهي، مان خوش آهيان.
sentences.roman: adī, shukur āhe, māṃ xushu āhiyāṃ.

lessons.title: Sorry, I didn't understand

tip.title: Sorry and no problem
tip.body:
- **معاف ڪجو** = sorry / excuse me (polite). To a friend: معاف ڪر.
- If you're lost: **مون کي سمجهه ۾ نه آيو** 'I didn't understand'.
- The reply to sorry or thanks: **ڪا ڳالهه ناهي** 'no problem'.
- **چڱو** 'OK, alright' and **ڀلي** 'sure, go ahead' close a conversation softly.

new: معاف ڪجو، مون کي سمجهه ۾ نه آيو.

sentences.native: مون کي سمجهه ۾ نه آيو، ادي.
sentences.roman: moṃ khe samajha meṃ na āyo, adī.

lessons.title: Welcome! Goodbye!

tip.title: Welcomes and goodbyes
tip.body:
- **ڀلي ڪري آيا** = welcome (lit. you came well) — the warm Sindhi way to greet a guest.
- **توهان سان ملي ڏاڍي خوشي ٿي** = very nice to meet you.
- To leave: **خدا حافظ** or **الله حافظ**, or **چڱو، پوءِ ملنداسين** 'OK, see you later'.
- **صبح بخير / شب بخير** (good morning / night) exist, but السلام عليڪم is far more common.
